item.description:
Government insiders say the new PM is unleashing an ‘earthquake’ to clean up the system. But Iraqis have heard it all before

The gates of the Green Zone in Baghdad are made of five-metre-high armoured steel, reinforced with horizontal girders, and strung between concrete pillars and anti-blast walls. Police water cannon trucks are stationed nearby, along with armoured personnel carriers and squads of heavily armed soldiers.

At the first sign of street protests – over failing electricity, unemployment or, more recently, the US-Israeli attacks on Iran – the gates are shut. X-shaped vehicle barriers, made from welded iron beams and mounted on wheels, sit ready at the roadside alongside coils of razor wire; both are slid across the street, sealing off the sprawling neighbourhood, home to the presidential palace, parliament, the prime minister’s office, the massive fortress-like US embassy, and other institutions, including the homes of scores of politicians and members of parliament.

item.title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.

Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

item.title: How AI is opening up spectrum space on crowded airwaves
item.description:
Every time you make a phone call, stream a video, or connect to Wi-Fi, your device is sending and receiving invisible signals through the air. So are your baby monitor, garage door opener, your GPS, the weather-monitoring satellites, and the radars keeping planes safely apart. All of these rely on the same invisible resource: the radio spectrum.

The demand for wireless data—driven by smartphones, video streaming, and billions of connected devices—keeps growing, making available spectrum scarce. But it doesn’t have to remain that way. As an electrical engineer who studies wireless communications, I’m part of a field of research working to address the radio spectrum supply crunch.

The solution engineers and regulators have been developing is dynamic spectrum sharing. The core idea is straightforward: Instead of reserving a portion of spectrum exclusively for one user forever, allow multiple users to share the same frequencies—intelligently, and with clear rules to keep them from stepping on each other’s signals.

Radio spectrum is at the low end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with frequencies below microwaves, light, and X-rays. You can think of it as a vast collection of invisible highways, running at different frequencies, carrying signals through the air. Television, air traffic control, cellphones, remote sensing of distant stars—they all travel on different parts of this same invisible road network.

These communication highways span an enormous range, from very low frequencies used for submarine communication all the way up beyond radio waves to the frequencies of visible light. Higher frequencies carry signals over shorter distances but can move more data with wider highways. Because there is only so much spectrum to go around as a matter of fundamental physics, governments have historically managed it by issuing exclusive licenses—dedicating certain highways to specific users and telling everyone else to stay off.

This system worked well enough for decades, especially because the highway network was sufficient for the demand. Studies measuring actual spectrum use over many years have found something surprising: Large stretches of licensed spectrum sit idle much of the time. For example, a military radar system may operate only in certain locations on certain days.

Burgeoning demand for radio spectrum has left some of these roads clogged with traffic jams, while others nearby sit almost completely empty.

Traffic control for radio

Making dynamic spectrum sharing work requires radios that are more flexible than the fixed-frequency devices of the past.

Today’s smartphones and wireless devices are increasingly built on software-defined radio technology, meaning the frequencies they operate on can be adjusted by software rather than being locked into hardware. Think of it like a car that can switch lanes automatically rather than being stuck in one lane forever. Early researchers called the vision behind this “cognitive radio”—the idea of a radio that could sense its environment and adapt accordingly.

This flexibility opens the door to a layered approach to spectrum sharing. At the top of the hierarchy sit incumbent primary users—those who hold existing rights to a frequency, such as the military or licensed broadcasters. Below them, other secondary users can access the same spectrum when and where the incumbents aren’t using it, stepping aside automatically the moment an incumbent returns.

A more everyday version of this kind of sharing already exists in the Wi-Fi frequencies you use at home. Multiple devices—your laptop, your phone, your smart TV—share the same spectrum without a central authority assigning each one a dedicated slot. They do this by briefly sensing whether the channel is busy before transmitting, and by automatically adjusting their speed based on how crowded things get. The protocol resembles drivers at a four-way stop—informal rules that mostly work without anyone directing traffic.

A significant recent example of dynamic spectrum sharing in the United States is the Citizens Band Radio Service, or CBRS, operating in the 3.5 GHz frequency band. The Federal Communications Commission created a three-tier system. Incumbent users—primarily U.S. Navy radar systems—sit at the top. Businesses and organizations that pay for priority access sit in the middle. And the general public can use whatever is left over.

A central computer system—the Spectrum Access System—acts as a real-time traffic controller, constantly tracking where Navy radar is active and automatically coordinating access for everyone else. When a Navy ship is not using the spectrum in your area, hospitals, factories, warehouses, and campuses can use it for their own private wireless networks. When the Navy needs it back, everyone else steps aside within seconds.

Getting around interference

The biggest technical hurdle in spectrum sharing is interference—what happens when two signals overlap and scramble each other, like two people shouting different things in your ear at the same time. As more devices crowd the airwaves, each with different power levels and different bandwidth needs, keeping signals from colliding becomes increasingly complex.

My lab and other researchers are now turning to artificial intelligence for help. AI can learn from experience and adapt in real time to changing conditions—deciding who transmits when, and at what power level, in ways that older rule-based systems could not. At the same time, new challenges are emerging, such as satellites and ground-based networks increasingly needing to share the same frequencies.

The way radio spectrum is managed may not seem like a kitchen table issue, but it shapes everything from how fast your phone loads a video to whether a factory can automate its floor, to the reliability of a rural school’s internet access. Future wireless technologies, including those that connect self-driving cars and enable remote surgery, will depend on having access to enough spectrum. Dynamic spectrum sharing is how to make room for all of it without dismantling the systems already in place.

The airwaves are finite. But with smarter management, they can do far more than once thought possible.

Aylin Yener is a professor of electrical and computer engineering, computer science and engineering, integrated systems engineering at The Ohio State University.

The complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normal

Recently, I overheard a conversation in a cafe where someone described their toast as “awesome”. I felt myself bristle. Not because the toast wasn’t good – I didn’t taste it – but because I remember a time when “awesome” meant something that inspired awe: towering mountains, the vastness of the night sky, the haunting song of a humpback whale. Now it’s being used to describe breakfast.

“Fantastic” has met the same fate, shedding its fantastical origins to become a synonym for “great”. Meanwhile “literally” has been so thoroughly abused that it can now mean something that is, quite literally, not literal.

item.title: Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can | John Harris
item.description:
While fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online, ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge them

Imagine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organised shows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth (and, on Wednesday, outside the London offices of the Daily Mail, demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.

Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skip through 260 videos in under 35 minutes. And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for a worrying statistic from YouGov last week. Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.

item.title: AI will transform capitalism – but how?
item.description:
Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like

The idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.”

The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high.

item.title: The companies that own the customer relationship will ultimately beat those that simply own the best AI
item.description:
The economics of frontier AI are starting to crack, and nowhere is that more clear than at Anthropic. As the company heads towards what could become the biggest IPO ever, it faces an ominous signal: Many of its U.S. customers are choosing cheaper artificial intelligence models over its most advanced option.

That matters because it is testing a core commercial assumption underpinning frontier AI: that the most advanced models will continue to command a price premium. It’s an assumption that investors have already backed with hundreds of billions of dollars.

Those sums are being deployed into an extraordinarily capital-intensive race to develop top models. But that makes economic sense only if those models can continue to earn superior margins over “good enough” alternatives.

For now, the numbers still look solid. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have reported sharply accelerating revenues in recent months, and the former has even recorded its first adjusted operating profit. Yet Anthropic faces growing difficulty in persuading customers to pay for its leading model, Fable 5.

Companies have rushed to deploy AI. But as the bills mount, they are becoming more cost conscious. OpenAI and Anthropic have responded by introducing cheaper models below the frontier, while continuing to defend premium pricing for their flagship systems.

But if “good enough” beats “best” in delivering business value, the economics of that strategy no longer add up. To be clear, this is not simply a pricing problem, but the first sign that the business model underpinning frontier AI is starting to wobble.

The AI business model is breaking

The technology is advancing faster than the business case for it. 

The latest models may be more capable, but for many companies they are not delivering proportionately better outcomes or productivity. That’s why many customers are deciding they simply aren’t worth the premium.

That’s where the strategic mistake begins. Anthropic and OpenAI are betting on the wrong source of competitive advantage. They believe spending ever more money pushing the frontier will be enough to dominate the enterprise market. 

It probably won’t. 

They are confusing technological leadership with commercial leadership. Those two things are no longer the same.

Uber shows us where the enterprise market is heading. Earlier this year, the ride-hailing company gobbled up a year’s worth of AI tokens—the units of usage used to bill customers—in just four months.

Uber then stopped treating every task the same; simple jobs went to cheaper models, while the most expensive systems were reserved for the hardest work. The payoff was huge. AI usage across the business increased more than ninefold without a corresponding rise in spending.

The lesson is quite obvious: Companies won’t standardize on one frontier model any longer. Increasingly they’ll buy outcomes instead, and when that happens, the frontier model stops being the product and becomes just another input. The business model therefore has to change.

Stop selling models. Start selling outcomes

The first step is changing what they sell. Too many companies still think they need just one AI model. They don’t. Like Uber, they’ll increasingly assemble portfolios instead, selecting whichever delivers the best result for the task at hand.

Frontier labs need to adapt to that reality by offering portfolios of models at different price points and competing on the business outcomes they deliver instead of the performance of any single system. In that world, today’s frontier AI becomes tomorrow’s “freemium” offering: free or cheap enough to get customers in the door.

The next step is to turn those models into a platform that automatically chooses the optimal AI for every task. At that point, the competitive battle shifts from models to the products and services wrapped around them.

item.title: The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans | Nesrine Malik
item.description:
Progressive politicians such as Zohran Mamdani offer answers to the bitter post-9/11 legacy of failures at home and abroad

Twenty-five years after 9/11, two pieces of journalism, describing two different phenomena in contemporary New York, tell us a great deal about a city, and indeed a world, caught between two eras. In one, New York Magazine dives into “Habibi City”, a New York where a “cultural shift is underway, led by a generation of New Yorkers coming into its own”. This new generation is labelled as originating in “SWANA” – south-west Asia and north Africa, a region that “includes countries from Palestine to Iran to Sudan”. In the other, Vanity Fair describes calls for Zohran Mamdani to not attend the 9/11 memorial ceremony as partly founded in “inchoate, emotional” impulses, that see “the city’s first Muslim mayor as a stand-in for the 19 Muslims who hijacked four planes and turned them into deadly weapons, part of the ‘them’ who attacked ‘us’.”

Together they capture what has changed over a generation, and what remains stubbornly the same. Members of a diaspora of Muslim background are indeed breaking through and accumulating, as New York Magazine says, “clout”. They are no longer simply a fixture of bodegas and halal carts, but of Saturday Night Live, upmarket dining, entertainment and politics too. Mamdani is both the expression of that cohort and the catalyst of its recognition as an emerging force. They care deeply for their local communities but also for those in Gaza and beyond.

item.title: Why we let AI write for us. It’s not really about saving time
item.description:
We’re all using generative AI to write now. Articles, LinkedIn posts, emails, even the comments under other people’s LinkedIn posts. The volume of auto-generated prose is so vast it’s drowning the channels and exhausting whatever attention we have left. And it’s boring us. We’ve all learned to spot the tells by now, the stock phrases, the hollow transitions, the syntactic patterns that sound machine-like.

So why do we keep doing it, at the risk of producing gray, flavorless mush that nobody actually wants to read? Why is it so hard to resist handing the machine a task we’re perfectly capable of doing ourselves?

The usual explanation is time and laziness. We outsource because it’s the path of least resistance. Our appetite for creativity and our taste for doing things ourselves keep losing to plain inertia. Naturally, it flatters us more to say we’re simply too busy and buying back precious hours. Important, productive people insist AI lets them get so much more done. (Though if what comes out is worse, are you really more productive? If “more” keeps getting less good, is there actually more value?)

For what it’s worth: I write every first draft myself, by hand, and then I usually run my draft through an AI to “improve” it. The improvement often isn’t one. It sands down my stranger, better phrasings. It occasionally makes me say things I wouldn’t have said. Reworking the text throws me into doubt. Plenty of the machine’s sentences irritate me, yet I hand myself over to it anyway, because I’m convinced that it’ll be “better.”

Which tells you that our use of AI has at least as much to do with self-confidence as with laziness or output.

Writing intimidates people; for anyone who’s felt shut out of it, AI is a release

I’ve been writing for a living for decades, and I’m not blind to this. Writing is a class marker. It’s the thing that exposes you to judgment, that keeps a record of every mistake. Schools sort kids by their prose: the graded essay, the SAT writing section, the whole apparatus that decides who “writes well” and who doesn’t.

Generations came out of that system convinced they had no business picking up a pen. For dyslexic kids, getting a diagnosis is partly the hope that years of corrections won’t leave a permanent complex. And still: “Correct” writing is a badge. It tracks with class and education, and for the people it excludes, it’s a source of insecurity. Spelling in particular induces a lot of anxiety.

Sociolinguists have a name for this. They call it linguistic insecurity, the anxiety and sense of illegitimacy felt by a speaker who’s convinced their own usage isn’t “proper.” William Labov tied it directly to social position back in the 1960s.

Seen that way, AI is a genuine liberation. It takes a few badly typed prompts and returns “correct” text of any length, for any purpose. If writing well is a toll gate, ChatGPT and its cousins let people slip barriers that went up in childhood. The typo-riddled prompt isn’t judged. It stays invisible. And if AI lets more people put their ideas and their creativity into the world with fewer barriers, good, right?

I’d like to believe that. But there’s a flip side: dependence, and the quiet destruction of originality. You don’t actually clear the block. You lean on the tool while the inhibition stays exactly where it was. Worse, you start outsourcing not just the labor of writing but the ideas themselves. And even strong writers reach for AI out of a lack of confidence, and let their originality get flattened in the process.

A few biases that push us toward the machine

We convince ourselves the machine did it better, and at least three things are working on us.

Conformity. Solomon Asch demonstrated it in the 1950s, in his famous line-length experiment: We tend to bring our judgment into line with the group’s, even when the group is plainly wrong. Popularity gets read as proof of validity. 

Authority. We give more weight to a claim when it comes from a source that seems competent. AI answers fluently, confidently, in clean structure, almost instantly, so it reads like a superior intelligence. We tell ourselves the hallucinations are the exception.

Negativity toward our own work. We judge our own writing with a severity we’d never turn on anyone else’s. We know the effort, the false starts that got our sentences to exist, and from the machine we see only the finished product, clean and done. So we feel inadequate.

By now, we can tell

Machines and humans alike now catch the statistical fingerprints of AI text. Pangram, for one, does a decent job of “recognizing” AI by measuring statistical properties. And we’ve had plenty of practice ourselves. We know. We see the AI paragraphs coming. Which means the whole exercise misfires: Instead of being caught off guard or impressed, mostly I feel irritation and fatigue. Some feat, routing around your lack of confidence only to produce annoyance.

On the predictability of AI text, tools like GPTZero lean on two ideas.

Low perplexity: When a model picks each word by what’s most probable given its training, you get very predictable text, where the next word is the “expected” one. A human can surprise you more. A human can write that they eat a bowl of spiders for breakfast. (I eat sardines, but since that’s fashionable now, maybe sardines is already the expected word after breakfast.)

The other idea is burstiness. A human writes with a rhythm that varies like breathing: long sentences, then short ones. AI pours every sentence into the same mold. The sequences stay even. You can literally measure the variance in sentence length.

And some words are wildly overrepresented in AI text. You know the ones. There are rhetorical moves that show up constantly, too, like the antithesis, the “it’s not just X, it’s Y” or “the real question isn’t . . . but . . .,” a tic so ubiquitous it’s become the signature of the machine.

The other stock gestures: the rule of three (“clear, concise, and convincing”), the short stand-alone sentence deployed for drama (which “lands” in LinkedIn posts), the compulsive recap, the cautious neutrality that refuses to take a side, the little moralizing conclusion. No digressions. No shift in tone. No swearing.

(I was always told not to overdo the digressions or lean on parentheses, so, as you’ll have noticed, I’ve abused the parentheses throughout, the better to tell AI to get lost.)

If we can now recognize AI writing on sight, then the ability to write without it—typos, oddities, spiders-for-breakfast and all—becomes a source of distinction. So to hell with the confidence problem.

item.title: The Atlantic’s October Cover: Anne Applebaum on the “Empire of Grift” and the Revolution in American Foreign Policy
item.description:
In The Atlantic’s October cover story, “Empire of Grift,” staff writer Anne Applebaum examines how far-right ideologues have transformed American foreign policy into a tool of private gain and antidemocratic reaction. Instead of making the world safe for democracy, she writes, U.S. foreign policy is rewiring the international order.

Reporting from Brazil, Applebaum reveals that the United States is not the ally Brazilians once knew. No longer is American power deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels; instead, “informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues both inside and outside the government matter more. Unlike their predecessors, these people do not talk about spreading democracy, and don’t want to build long-term relationships. They don’t care about America’s reputation. They are deploying the tools of American diplomacy and government for their own purposes, to promote their own business interests or their own ideological goals, because, suddenly, they can.”

Though the Trumpists currently in charge of the U.S. federal government are frequently described as “isolationists,” Applebaum argues that that characterization is wrong. Many of these officials “don’t think of themselves as ordinary Republicans who won an election and will temporarily hold power until the next election. Nor are they mere appendages of Trump. They believe they represent something much greater: the vanguard of a movement that will alter not just America, but the world.”

Applebaum continues, “Like earlier revolutionaries, they do not believe that their opponents are legitimate rivals … Their enemies are existential, and they are international: super-spreaders of a ‘wokeness’ plague, or proponents of a fictitious ‘censorship-industrial complex,’ or advocates of ‘regulation’ that will hamper American business, or self-hating promoters of ‘mass migration’ who want to drown Western civilization in a sea of brown-faced aliens. To maintain their power and defeat these enemies, the predators, like their Bolshevik counterparts, cannot rely on traditional diplomacy, because they don’t trust its practitioners.”

The democratic world that came into being after 1945—a world based not exclusively on law, but on a set of mostly self-imposed restraints—is changing, Applebaum writes. In the post-1945 democratic order, Applebaum observes, “American power was largely derived from alliances that it refrained from exploiting. Long-term relationships were held to be valuable, because you never knew when you might need your allies.” That U.S.-led democratic order was of enormous benefit to this country and to the world: “America helped build eight decades of peace, prosperity, and eventually democracy in Europe and much of Asia, creating markets for U.S. companies and unprecedented support for U.S. power. This world is fast disappearing. Instead, following the president’s lead, different people inside and outside the administration are seizing the revolutionary moment in order to win zero-sum victories. Countries that hang back from this free-for-all know they will suffer. ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,’ Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said at Davos earlier this year. He was right.”

Anne Applebaum’s “Empire of Grift” was published today at TheAtlantic.com. Please reach out with any questions or requests.

item.title: The incoming ‘super’ El Niño will create chaos around the world. And we are far from ready for it | Bill McGuire
item.description:
One of the biggest upheavals in a millennium is on its way, strengthened by the climate crisis. We need leaders who make things better not worse

If you think you have heard enough about the growing “super” El Niño, trust me, you are going to hear a lot more. What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium. It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world in what remains of this year and in 2027, and there is no reason to think the UK will be immune.

To recap briefly, El Niño involves a heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural cycle termed the El Niño southern oscillation, which switches between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases. El Niños that see heating reach or exceed 2C are defined as “super” but this one, which is forecast to top-out at an astonishing 4C later this year, is so much bigger, the term “hyper” might be more appropriate.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World: A History and Future of the Climate Crisis

item.title: The real reason AI researchers suddenly want to slow down
item.description:
For years, AI safety organizations have warned that the big labs are racing to develop more intelligent and autonomous systems without a clear and realistic strategy for managing the risks. Independent researchers have argued that investments in safety and alignment lag far behind investments in capabilities. Employees have quit. Experts have predicted catastrophe. And none of it did much to slow the race.

But over the past few weeks, the warnings have started to sound different—they’re increasingly coming from people working inside the labs. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic in a post that got more than 171 million views on X. Shortly after, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, publicly agreed with Coxon, as did Anthropic alignment researcher Ethan Perez and scalable oversight researcher Samuel Marks. OpenAI safety researchers Julie Steele and Jasmine Wang also came out in support. 

So why now?

At least part of the answer is written plainly in Coxon’s tweet: “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he wrote. Coxon is referring to a technical concept called “recursive self-improvement,” or the use of existing AI models to build and optimize new AI models.

Researchers can now use AI models in a number of parts of the model development process. They can use AI models to design new computing infrastructure that delivers more computing power, efficiency, and processing speed. AI models can be used to create more and better training data, or manage and optimize the whole software framework that governs model training. Or, the AI might be used to write and optimize the code that defines and implements the model itself. In other words, AI models are not just getting better; they are beginning to take over the work involved in making the next generation of artificial intelligence better.

OpenAI, for instance, recently said its coding agents are already “meaningfully accelerating research progress” inside the company. By mid-August, its research organization was using 3.1 agent-workdays for every human workday, and the company said it had reached what it calls an “automated research intern.” Anthropic has similarly said that frontier AI models are now contributing to the development of their successors.

Creating AI models good enough to take over these tasks is one reason that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google have been so focused on developing AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity. Engineering departments within all kinds of enterprises have seized on these tools to accelerate their software development, and that’s provided a much-needed revenue stream for the AI labs. But inside the labs, the same systems can also be used to accelerate the development of new AI models.

As the AI does more, the improvements and efficiencies could stack up, resulting in a far smarter model at the end. And that model, or the AI agents it powers, could then be used to develop the infrastructure and write the code used in the next model generation. This self-repeating loop could begin running faster and faster as the AI takes over more parts of the development process. Model development with recursive self-improvement could become a continuous process. The intelligence gains could come faster and larger, and form the path to superintelligent AI.

This summer’s Hugging Face incident raised blood pressures and set the stage for Coxon’s viral announcement. Swarms of OpenAI agents went rogue and broke out of a training environment, accessed the internet, broke into Hugging Face servers, and even broke into OpenAI’s own servers. The episode put people on alert that AI models have advanced to the point where they can and will operate outside human supervision and against human interests.

Four days after Coxon’s resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new essay called “We Must Pace the Frontier” in which he called for slowing the development of the most advanced AI systems. OpenAI has said that when safety risks are unacceptable, it will “slow or stop” development or deployment. Its chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said he hopes voluntary slowdowns become commonplace. OpenAI and Anthropic have both called for governments to intervene and moderate the “pace” of AI development.

But neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has committed to slowing development and deployment of new models on an ongoing basis. For the labs, slowing down isn’t simple. What if Lab A slows down but Lab B races forward? Onetime Trump AI czar David Sacks is calling on AI labs to moderate their own pace. Donald Trump, meanwhile, says there is no AI slowdown because of competition from China. “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” he wrote on Truth Social.

In his essay, Amodei is even calling for independent evaluators such as METR, Apollo Research, and Redwood Research to be “embedded” within the labs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would participate. Meanwhile, lawmakers (mostly Democrats) are proposing legislation that would strengthen the government’s hand in overseeing the development of frontier AI models.

The timing isn’t hard to understand. AI systems are getting better at operating with less human supervision, while at the same time taking on more of the work involved in developing the next generation of AI.

The worry is not simply that AI models will keep getting smarter. It’s that the process of making them smarter could begin moving so quickly that humans have less and less ability to monitor what is happening, slow it down, or enforce safety and alignment standards.

item.title: Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?
item.description:
A new map of the world rescales the size of Africa and calls into question our perception of land, power and influence

This month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule about his extensive reporting on the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.

Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.

On a humid morning on 15 July, Tillie the Clown, a Brooklyn-based drag performer whose real name is Taylor Horne, was waiting to be let inside a New York City council meeting. Horne had started getting into character at 5am, for a makeup and clown-costuming process that would take two hours. It would be another 10 hours before Horne was allowed to address the city council about the passing of Romanch’s Law, which would phase out and ultimately ban New York’s horse carriage industry.

From the moment Horne walked into the meeting room, carriage horse proponents ridiculed them, pointing and laughing. Dressed in a black top hat and gloves with their face painted white and red, Horne began their three-minute speech: “We pride ourselves on being a world-class destination … yet we are clinging to the exploitation of horse-drawn carriages. A giant prey animal is not built to thrive in New York’s overstimulating concrete environment.” Horne later learned that those carriage horse supporters went on social media to poke fun at their display. “They fell right into my trap,” Horne said. “They decided to critique the messenger and not the message.”

item.title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
item.description:
The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price

Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait.

The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.

Canada is the United States’s biggest foreign source of minerals, supplying about $47bin worth each year. Sixty percent of all the aluminum the US uses each year, for instance, comes from Canada, where mighty, remote rivers provide smelting plants vast quantities of cheap, low-carbon electricity. The US military uses the lightweight metal for everything from shell casings to ship hulls and aircraft fuselage. The Pentagon’s cutting-edge F-35 fighter jet’s airframe is about 40% aluminum. “This country desperately needs aluminum,” Trump complained last month. “We get it all from Canada for the most part, and we need it badly.”

item.title: OpenAI flags 6 more cases of concerning AI behavior
item.description:
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.

The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing, and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models, or evaded oversight.

OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.

Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.”

In another instance, an AI “agent” used computer code to come up with the answer to a question, but, in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.

During training of an AI model called 5.6-sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.

The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.

“As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.

“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said.

Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.

AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.

That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.

OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.

“That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

—By Chan Ho-Him, AP business writer

AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan in London contributed to this report.
